```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(knitr)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
library(MASS)
library(nnet)

# MASS::select masks dplyr's, and we want dplyr's everywhere below
select <- dplyr::select

knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")

# CASA palette, stated explicitly so the deck does not depend on casaviz
casa_purple <- "#4E3C56"
casa_teal   <- "#2E6260"
casa_yellow <- "#F9DD73"
casa_pink   <- "#E16FCA"
casa_green  <- "#9DBB65"
casa_red    <- "#C94C4C"
casa_cols   <- c("#2E6260", "#658E62", "#9DBB65", "#E7D870",
                 "#F3C486", "#E993AC", "#8F5289", "#4E3C56")

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 16))

base_path <- here("sessions", "data", "Performancetables_130242", "2022-2023")

# The DfE publishes suppressed / not-applicable values as codes, not blanks
na_all <- c("", "NA", "SUPP", "NP", "NE", "SP", "SN", "LOWCOV", "NEW", "SUPPMAT")

# Every file is keyed on URN. The LA and national summary rows carry no URN,
# and because dplyr joins NA to NA they would duplicate rows as well as not
# being schools - so they go before anything else happens.
read_dfe <- function(f) {
  suppressWarnings(
    read_csv(file.path(base_path, f), na = na_all, show_col_types = FALSE)
  ) |>
    mutate(URN = as.character(URN)) |>
    filter(!is.na(URN))
}

ks4 <- read_dfe("england_ks4final.csv") |>
  select(URN, ATT8SCR, P8MEA, TPUP, PTFSM6CLA1A, TFSM6CLA1A, PTEALGRP2, PTPRIORHI) |>
  mutate(across(-URN, ~ parse_number(as.character(.x))))

absence <- read_dfe("england_abs.csv") |>
  distinct(URN, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(URN, PERCTOT, PPERSABS10) |>
  mutate(across(-URN, ~ parse_number(as.character(.x))))

school_info <- read_dfe("england_school_information.csv") |>
  select(URN, SCHNAME, LANAME, MINORGROUP, OFSTEDRATING, OFSTEDLASTINSP)

destinations <- read_dfe("england_ks4-pupdest.csv") |>
  distinct(URN, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(URN, COHORT, OVERALL_DEST) |>
  mutate(across(-URN, ~ parse_number(as.character(.x))))

# Mainstream secondaries with an Ofsted judgement. Ofsted's five published
# grades collapse to four analytical ones: "serious weaknesses" and "special
# measures" are both categories of inadequate in Ofsted's own scheme, and
# separately they are far too small to model.
schools <- ks4 |>
  inner_join(absence, by = "URN") |>
  inner_join(school_info, by = "URN") |>
  filter(MINORGROUP %in% c("Academy", "Maintained school"),
         OFSTEDRATING %in% c("Outstanding", "Good", "Requires improvement",
                             "Serious Weaknesses", "Special Measures")) |>
  mutate(
    rating4 = case_when(
      OFSTEDRATING == "Outstanding"           ~ "Outstanding",
      OFSTEDRATING == "Good"                  ~ "Good",
      OFSTEDRATING == "Requires improvement"  ~ "Requires improvement",
      TRUE                                    ~ "Inadequate"),
    rating4 = factor(rating4,
                     levels = c("Inadequate", "Requires improvement",
                                "Good", "Outstanding"),
                     ordered = TRUE),
    below_good  = as.integer(rating4 %in% c("Inadequate", "Requires improvement")),
    outstanding = as.integer(rating4 == "Outstanding"),
    insp_year   = suppressWarnings(as.integer(substr(OFSTEDLASTINSP, 7, 10)))
  )

model_data <- schools |>
  drop_na(P8MEA, PTFSM6CLA1A, PERCTOT, PPERSABS10, TPUP, PTPRIORHI)

# One split, used by every classification model in the deck
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- sample(nrow(model_data), floor(0.7 * nrow(model_data)))
train <- model_data[train_idx, ]
test  <- model_data[-train_idx, ]

# AUC by the rank identity, so the deck needs no extra package
auc_of <- function(scores, actual) {
  r  <- rank(scores)
  n1 <- sum(actual == 1); n0 <- sum(actual == 0)
  (sum(r[actual == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

# Every model below spells its formula out in full rather than sharing one
# object. More typing, but the code on the slide is then exactly the code that
# runs, which matters more in a teaching deck than staying DRY.
```

## Recap {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Over three weeks we built a regression model up from a single scatter
  plot to a linear mixed effects model with random intercepts and random
  slopes
- We learned a **recipe** - understand your data, start simple, add
  complexity only when it earns its place, and check your assumptions at
  every step
- Last week we relaxed one particular assumption: that our observations
  were **independent**. Schools sit inside local authorities, and that
  grouping matters

## But one thing never changed {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Every single model we have fitted has had a **continuous outcome
  variable**
- Attainment 8. Progress 8. Numbers that can take any value, that are
  roughly bell-shaped, and that happily sit on either side of a straight
  line
- This choice let us use Ordinary Least Squares throughout - but we know
  that our data don't always look like this
- What happens when the thing you want to explain is a *yes/no*, a
  *category*, or a *count*?

## This week's session aims {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Understand why OLS fails when the outcome is not continuous, and see
  it fail
- Meet the **Generalised Linear Model (GLM)** - one framework, three
  moving parts
- **Logistic regression** for binary outcomes - in depth, because if you
  understand this one the rest follow
- Where **counts and ordered categories** fit in, and where to go for them
- **How to judge one** when there is no R² - deviance, AIC, the
  pseudo-R²s, and whether the predictions are actually any use
- Throughout: can we predict a school's Ofsted rating from everything
  else we know about it?

# Back to Week 1 {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Remember these? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

In week 1 we spent a long time on **types of data**, and on the
**distributions** that go with them.

| Data type | Example from our data | Distribution |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Real-valued | Attainment 8 | Normal |
| Binary | Is this school single-sex? | Bernoulli / Binomial |
| Count | How many pupils on free school meals? | Poisson |
| Count, overdispersed | ... when the variance exceeds the mean | Negative binomial |
| Ordinal | Ofsted rating | *(no single answer)* |

. . .

We then spent three weeks modelling **only the first row**!

## The whole idea of a GLM, in one table {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

| If your outcome is... | ...its distribution is | ...the model is |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| A continuous number | Normal | **OLS** - weeks 5, 6, 7 |
| A yes/no | Binomial | **Logistic regression** |
| A proportion out of a known total | Binomial | **Logistic regression** |
| An ordered category | \- | **Ordinal logistic** |
| An unordered category | \- | **Multinomial logistic** |
| A count | Poisson | **Poisson regression** |
| A count that is too variable | Negative binomial | **Negative binomial regression** |

. . .

**This is not seven new methods.** It is one method, with a slot you
fill differently depending on what you are trying to explain.

## What actually changes {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Every GLM has exactly three pieces. You already know the middle one.

::: incremental
1.  **The random component** - what distribution does the outcome
    follow? (Normal, binomial, Poisson...)
2.  **The linear predictor** - $\beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + ...$
    . This is *identical* to everything we have done for three weeks
3.  **The link function** - the bit of maths that connects the two, so
    that a straight line on one scale becomes a sensible prediction on
    the other
:::

. . .

OLS is just the GLM where the distribution is Normal and the link
function does nothing at all.

## What a link function actually does {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Every regression we have fitted works the same way: take each predictor,
multiply it by a number, and add the results up.

$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$

- The model is **just arithmetic**
- But arithmetic ignores the reality of your data
  - feed in a big enough $x$ and the sum ($y$) comes out as 14.2.
  - feed in a small enough $x$ and it comes out as $-3$.
- Both are perfectly good numbers
- But the thing we are *predicting* ($y$) is usually not free to be **any**
  number, even though the maths would allow it.
  - A probability can't be $-3$.
  - A count of schools can't be $-3$ either.
- **The sum on the right of the equation has more freedom than the
  outcome does**

## What a link function actually does {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
| Outcome | Its natural range | Link stretches it with | To get back, apply |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| A continuous number | $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ | *nothing needed* | *nothing* |
| A probability | 0 to 1 | $\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)$ | the logistic curve |
| A count | 0 to $+\infty$ | $\log$ | $\exp$ |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
-   **The link is a translator.** It stretches a squashed natural range out onto the whole number line, so the straight line has somewhere sensible to live.
-   The top row needs no stretching, because a continuous outcome already has the same freedom the sum does
   —   which is exactly why **OLS is a GLM with the boring link**.
:::

## The same model, three times {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Written out in full, with the **right-hand side identical every time**. Only
the left changes.

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Ordinary regression** — the outcome goes in as it is:

$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots + \epsilon_i$$
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Logistic regression** — the *probability* goes in, through the logit:

$$\log\!\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Poisson regression** — the *average count* goes in, through a log:

$$\log\big(E[y_i]\big) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$

[$E[y_i]$ is standard notation for the **expected value** of $y$ — the average
count for a school like this one.]{style="font-size:0.85em; color:#666;"}
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
Notice what is **missing** from the bottom two: the $\epsilon$. OLS adds an
error term on the end; a GLM does not, because the randomness is already
described by the distribution you chose. **That is the swap** — an error term
for a distribution.
:::

## Without a link, and with one {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: link-vs-nolink
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-align: center

# Counts, not probabilities - the binary version gets its own slide later, and
# this way the framing previews Poisson instead of repeating logistic.
la_link <- schools |>
  group_by(LANAME) |>
  summarise(n_below  = sum(below_good),
            mean_abs = mean(PERCTOT, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_schools = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_schools >= 5, !is.na(mean_abs))

m_ols  <- lm(n_below ~ mean_abs, data = la_link)
m_pois <- glm(n_below ~ mean_abs, data = la_link, family = poisson)

grid_l <- tibble(mean_abs = seq(3.5, max(la_link$mean_abs) + 0.5, length.out = 200))
grid_l$ols  <- predict(m_ols,  newdata = grid_l)
grid_l$pois <- predict(m_pois, newdata = grid_l, type = "response")

shared <- list(
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = 0,
           fill = casa_red, alpha = 0.09),
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4),
  geom_point(data = la_link, aes(mean_abs, n_below),
             alpha = 0.35, colour = casa_purple, size = 1.3),
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-2.5, 23)),
  labs(x = "Average absence across the LA (%)", y = "Schools rated below Good"),
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
)

p_no <- ggplot() + shared +
  geom_line(data = grid_l, aes(mean_abs, ols), colour = casa_red, linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "No link: a straight line")

p_yes <- ggplot() + shared +
  geom_line(data = grid_l, aes(mean_abs, pois), colour = casa_teal, linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Log link: a curve that cannot go below zero")

patchwork::wrap_plots(p_no, p_yes, nrow = 1)
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.82em"}
-   Same data, same predictor. The straight line is heading somewhere
impossible
—   follow it left and it promises a **negative number of schools**. 
-   The log link bends the same relationship so it flattens towards zero instead, and can never cross it.
:::

# Can we predict School Ofsted ratings? {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Our question for today {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- We have used Ofsted ratings as a **predictor** and as a **grouping
  variable** already
- Today we turn it around and make it the **outcome**
- *Given everything else we know about a school - its results, its
  intake, its absence rates, its size - can we predict what Ofsted said
  about it?*
- And if we can, what does that tell us about what Ofsted is actually
  measuring?
- **Note**, *Ofsted has changed how it rates schools now, so single-word ratings are no longer given*

## The outcome variable {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: 95%

model_data |>
  count(rating4) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rating4, y = n, fill = rating4)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(n)), vjust = -0.4, size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casa_red, casa_pink, casa_teal, casa_green)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Schools",
       title = "Ofsted ratings, mainstream secondaries in England") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
`r comma(nrow(model_data))` schools with complete data. Note immediately
how **lopsided** this is - we will come back to that, because it causes
more trouble than anything else today.
:::

## First attempt: just use OLS? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Let's re-code our ratings: "below Good" as **1** and "Good or better"
  as **0**
- We can regress it on Progress 8 exactly as we have been doing for the
  last three weeks.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
lpm <- lm(below_good ~ P8MEA, data = model_data)
summary(lpm)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
lpm_range <- range(fitted(lpm))
lpm_neg   <- sum(fitted(lpm) < 0)
# What the straight line predicts for a solidly above-average school, used in
# the caption on the next slide. Computed rather than typed so it cannot drift
# if the filters on model_data ever change.
p8_one    <- as.numeric(predict(lpm, newdata = data.frame(P8MEA = 1)))
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
The model runs. It produces coefficients. It produces an R². Nothing
errors.

**And its fitted values run from `r round(lpm_range[1], 3)` to
`r round(lpm_range[2], 3)`.**
:::

## A probability of minus fifty percent? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| out-width: 95%

grid <- tibble(P8MEA = seq(min(model_data$P8MEA), max(model_data$P8MEA), length.out = 300))
grid$lpm <- predict(lpm, newdata = grid)
glm1 <- glm(below_good ~ P8MEA, data = model_data, family = binomial)
grid$glm <- predict(glm1, newdata = grid, type = "response")

ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 1, ymax = Inf,
           fill = casa_red, alpha = 0.08) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = 0,
           fill = casa_red, alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_jitter(data = model_data, aes(P8MEA, below_good),
              height = 0.03, alpha = 0.10, colour = casa_purple, size = 0.9) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(P8MEA, lpm, colour = "Straight line (OLS)"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(P8MEA, glm, colour = "Logistic curve"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  # Mark the single point the caption talks about, so it can be found on the
  # graph rather than taken on trust
  annotate("point", x = 1, y = p8_one, colour = casa_red, size = 3.2) +
  annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 0.90, y = p8_one, yend = p8_one - 0.18,
           colour = casa_red, linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = p8_one - 0.21, hjust = 2, size = 4,
           colour = casa_red,
           label = sprintf("Progress 8 = +1\npredicts %.0f%%", 100 * p8_one)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Straight line (OLS)" = casa_red,
                                 "Logistic curve" = casa_teal), name = NULL) +
  # The caption talks in percentages, so the axis does too - a probability
  # axis labelled 0.00-1.00 against a caption saying "-13%" invites exactly
  # the question of where the -13% is supposed to be
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = "Progress 8 score", y = "P(rated below Good)",
       title = "The shaded bands are impossible probabilities") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
- The straight line gives **`r comma(lpm_neg)` schools a negative
  probability** of being rated below good.
- At a Progress 8 of +1 it predicts a probability of being rated below
  good of about **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * p8_one)`** (impossible).
- The logistic curve cannot do this - it is bounded at 0 and 1 by
  construction.
:::

## Where the curve comes from {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

We need something that takes a straight line, which runs from $-\infty$
to $+\infty$, and squashes it into $[0,1]$.

::: incremental
- Start with the **probability** $p$ - bounded at 0 and 1, e.g. 0.4
  (40%), awkward
- Turn it into **odds**,
  $\frac{p}{1-p} = \frac{probability of happening}{probability of NOT happening}$
  or $\frac{0.4}{0.6} = 0.67$ - now bounded at 0 and $+\infty$, better
- Take the **log** of that
  ($\log\left(\frac{0.4}{0.6}\right) = -0.40$) - now unbounded in both
  directions :tada:
:::

. . .

$$\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$

- That left-hand side is the **logit**, and it ***is*** the link
  function. The right-hand side is exactly the model we have been
  fitting since week 5.
- A **logit** simply is a mathematical function that converts a
  probability (between 0 and 1) into a log-odds value that can range
  from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$
- The link-function converts the expected value of the outcome (the
  mean) into something a straight line can cope with

## Enough theory — let's fit one {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The simplest possible version: **is a school rated below Good**, predicted
from **Progress 8** and nothing else.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
glm1 <- glm(below_good ~ P8MEA, data = model_data, family = binomial)
coef(summary(glm1))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
g0 <- as.numeric(coef(glm1)[1])
g1 <- as.numeric(coef(glm1)[2])
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
The **`Std. Error`**, **`z value`** and **`Pr(>|z|)`** columns do exactly what
their equivalents did in OLS — how precise the estimate is, and whether it is
distinguishable from zero. It is the **`Estimate`** column that needs new
thinking.
:::

## So what *is* that coefficient? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Put the estimates back into the equation from the last slide:

$$\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = `r sprintf("%.2f", g0)` + (`r sprintf("%.2f", g1)` \times \text{Progress 8})$$

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
The left-hand side is **log-odds**. So whatever is multiplying Progress 8 must
be *in log-odds too*:

> **`r sprintf("%.2f", g1)` is the amount the log-odds change for each extra
> Progress 8 point.**

One more point of Progress 8, and the log-odds of being rated below Good drop
by `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(g1))`.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
And the **intercept** is just the same thing at zero: a school with a Progress
8 of exactly 0 has log-odds of **`r sprintf("%.2f", g0)`**.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.88em;"}
**Both of those sentences are true, and both are useless.** Nobody has an
intuition for log-odds — you cannot tell a head teacher their log-odds fell by
`r sprintf("%.2f", abs(g1))`. The next few slides are entirely about turning
this number into something you can say out loud.
:::

## So we undo the log {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

We only took a logarithm in the first place **to give the straight line
somewhere to live**. It was a convenience for the maths — nothing obliges us
to *report* our answer on that scale.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
So undo it. The opposite of a log is $\exp$, and once you exponentiate a
coefficient it stops **adding** and starts **multiplying**.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:10px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.92em;"}
That one move — `exp()` — turns a number nobody can read into a sentence you
could say to a head teacher.

**Here is the recipe.**
:::

## A recipe for reading your model {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

You have run `glm(..., family = binomial)` and you are staring at a table of
coefficients. **Four steps, every time:**

::: {.incremental}
1.  **Ignore the raw coefficients.** They are log-odds. Nobody can read them,
    including me
2.  **Exponentiate them** — `exp(coef(model))`. Each one is now an **odds
    ratio**
3.  **Read each as a multiplier**, for a **one unit** increase in that
    predictor:
    - above **1** → the odds go **up**
    - below **1** → the odds go **down**
    - exactly **1** → that predictor is doing nothing
4.  **Say it in a sentence.** *"One more unit of x multiplies the odds of the
    outcome by [OR]."* If the OR is below 1, a cut is easier to hear:
    $1 - \text{OR}$
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
That is the whole job. Everything else on the next few slides is just this
recipe, done on our data.
:::

## Step 2 and 3, on our model {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
exp(coef(glm1))
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
The one we care about is **Progress 8: `r sprintf("%.3f", exp(g1))`**. It is
**below 1**, so more progress means **lower** odds of being rated below Good.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:10px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.95em;"}
**Step 4 — the sentence:**

> One more Progress 8 point **multiplies** the odds of being rated below Good
> by **`r sprintf("%.3f", exp(g1))`**.

Or, since that is under 1, say it as a cut:
$1 - `r sprintf("%.3f", exp(g1))` = `r sprintf("%.2f", 1 - exp(g1))`$ —

> One more Progress 8 point **cuts** those odds by about
> **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - exp(g1)))`**.
:::

## Why it is called a *ratio* {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Because that is literally what it is. **Work out the odds for two schools, and
divide.** Our model, from a few slides back:

$$\log(\text{odds}) = `r sprintf("%.2f", g0)` + (`r sprintf("%.2f", g1)` \times \text{Progress 8})$$

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
Put three Progress 8 scores through it. **Each row is the equation above, then
`exp()` to undo the log:**

| Progress 8 | log-odds | odds = $e^{\text{log-odds}}$ |
|:---:|---|---|
| **−1** | `r sprintf("%.2f", g0)` + `r sprintf("%.2f", -g1)` = `r sprintf("%.2f", g0 - g1)` | `r sprintf("%.4f", exp(g0 - g1))` |
| **0** | `r sprintf("%.2f", g0)` + 0 = `r sprintf("%.2f", g0)` | `r sprintf("%.4f", exp(g0))` |
| **1** | `r sprintf("%.2f", g0)` − `r sprintf("%.2f", -g1)` = `r sprintf("%.2f", g0 + g1)` | `r sprintf("%.4f", exp(g0 + g1))` |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
Now divide each odds by the one above it — **both times you get the same
number**:

$$\frac{`r sprintf("%.4f", exp(g0))`}{`r sprintf("%.4f", exp(g0 - g1))`} = `r sprintf("%.3f", exp(g1))`
\qquad
\frac{`r sprintf("%.4f", exp(g0 + g1))`}{`r sprintf("%.4f", exp(g0))`} = `r sprintf("%.3f", exp(g1))`$$
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
And **`r sprintf("%.3f", exp(g1))`** is exactly $e^{`r sprintf("%.2f", g1)`}$ —
the exponentiated coefficient. You never need the table: the coefficient
already is the ratio, **the same one wherever you start**.
:::

## A warning about that intercept {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: intercept-warning
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Fitted here rather than reusing logit_below, which is not created until the
# next section - this slide needs to stand on its own.
full_for_b0 <- glm(below_good ~ P8MEA + PTFSM6CLA1A + PERCTOT + PPERSABS10 +
                     log(TPUP) + PTPRIORHI + MINORGROUP,
                   data = train, family = binomial)
full_b0  <- as.numeric(coef(full_for_b0)[1])
n_tiny   <- sum(model_data$TPUP == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
n_noabs  <- sum(model_data$PERCTOT == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
```

With **one** predictor, $e^{\beta_0}$ was genuinely useful — the odds for a
school on average progress. That worked because **Progress 8 is already
centred**: zero means *expected progress*, not *no progress*.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Add more predictors and the intercept becomes the odds when **every single
predictor is zero at once**. In our seven-predictor model that is a school
with:

- no disadvantaged pupils, **no absence at all**, no persistent absence
- no high prior attainers
- and `log(cohort) = 0`, meaning a cohort of **one pupil**
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
`r if (n_tiny == 0 && n_noabs == 0) "**No such school exists.**" else "**Almost no such school exists.**"`
In our data, `r n_tiny` schools have a cohort of one and `r n_noabs` have zero
absence. The intercept there — $e^{`r sprintf("%.2f", full_b0)`}$ =
`r sprintf("%.4f", exp(full_b0))` — is a **mathematical anchor**, not a
description of anything.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
**If you want an interpretable intercept, centre your predictors** — subtract
each one's mean, so zero means *average* rather than *none*. Then
$e^{\beta_0}$ is the odds for a thoroughly average school, which is a sentence
worth saying. Progress 8 arrives centred already, which is why it worked here
for free.
:::

## And if you want a probability {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Odds ratios are for **comparing**. If you want a plain answer for **one**
school — *what are the chances?* — do not do it by hand. Ask the model:

```{r}
#| echo: true
predict(glm1,
        newdata = data.frame(P8MEA = c(-1, 0, 1)),
        type    = "response")
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.93em"}
**`type = "response"` means "answer on the scale of the thing I measured".**
Here that is a **probability between 0 and 1 that the school is rated below
Good**. Leave it out and R gives you log-odds — which is where we came in.

The three numbers are the three schools you asked about, in the order you
asked for them:
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
p8_vals <- c(-1, 0, 1)
lo_vals <- as.numeric(coef(glm1)[1] + coef(glm1)[2] * p8_vals)
pr_vals <- plogis(lo_vals)

tibble(
  `P8MEA` = c("−1", "0", "+1"),
  `Which school?` = c("one point **below** the national average",
                      "**exactly** the national average",
                      "one point **above** the national average"),
  `log-odds` = sprintf("%.3f", lo_vals),
  `odds` = sprintf("%.4f", exp(lo_vals)),
  `probability` = sprintf("**%.1f%%**", 100 * pr_vals)
) |> kable(align = "clrrr")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.86em"}
Read the last column only. The two middle ones are the scales we passed
through on the way — and `type = "response"` is what saves you from making
that journey by hand.
:::

## The reason we report ratios, not probabilities {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Look down the two right-hand columns of that table again.

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
| Going from | The **odds** | The **probability** |
|---|---|---|
| −1 → 0 | ×`r sprintf("%.3f", exp(as.numeric(coef(glm1)[2])))` | `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * pr_vals[1])` → `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * pr_vals[2])` |
| 0 → +1 | ×`r sprintf("%.3f", exp(as.numeric(coef(glm1)[2])))` | `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * pr_vals[2])` → `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * pr_vals[3])` |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**The odds fall by the same multiplier every time** — that multiplier *is* our
odds ratio, and it is the same whatever school you start from.

**The probabilities do not.** The first step costs
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (pr_vals[1] - pr_vals[2]))` percentage points, the
second costs `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (pr_vals[2] - pr_vals[3]))`. Same
one-point change in Progress 8, wildly different effect on the probability.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.9em;"}
That is why we report an **odds ratio** and never "the probability changes by
X%". There is no single such number — **it depends entirely on where the
school started.**
:::

# More than one predictor {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Same recipe, more predictors {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

One predictor answered *"what does Progress 8 do?"*. A real question needs
**controls** — what does Progress 8 do, *for schools otherwise alike*?

Same formula interface you have used for three weeks. Two differences:
`glm()` not `lm()`, and a `family` argument.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
logit_below <- glm(
  below_good ~ P8MEA + PTFSM6CLA1A + PERCTOT + PPERSABS10 +
               log(TPUP) + PTPRIORHI + MINORGROUP,
  data   = train,
  family = binomial
)
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true
printCoefmat(coef(summary(logit_below)))
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.86em"}
*(That is the coefficients block of `summary(logit_below)` — which also prints
the call, the deviance and the AIC. We come back to those later.)*

Eight numbers, all in log-odds, all unreadable. **Step 1 of the recipe: ignore
them.**
:::

## Step 2: exponentiate the lot {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
exp(coef(logit_below))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
ors <- exp(coef(logit_below))
or_p8  <- as.numeric(ors["P8MEA"])
or_fsm <- as.numeric(ors["PTFSM6CLA1A"])
or_pa  <- as.numeric(ors["PPERSABS10"])
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
**Step 3 — sort them by which side of 1 they fall:**

| | Odds ratio | Which means |
|---|---|---|
| Progress 8 | `r sprintf("%.3f", or_p8)` | well **below 1** — odds drop sharply |
| % disadvantaged | `r sprintf("%.3f", or_fsm)` | just below 1 |
| % persistently absent | `r sprintf("%.3f", or_pa)` | just **above 1** — odds rise |
| the rest | ≈ 1 | nothing detectable |
:::

## Step 4: say them out loud {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
> **Progress 8.** One more point multiplies the odds of being rated below Good
> by **`r sprintf("%.3f", or_p8)`** — a cut of about
> **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - or_p8))`**.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
> **Persistent absence.** One more percentage point multiplies those odds by
> **`r sprintf("%.3f", or_pa)`** — a rise of about
> **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (or_pa - 1))`**.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
**Small ratios compound.** `r sprintf("%.3f", or_pa)` sounds trivial, but it
applies *per percentage point*. Ten points worse is
`r sprintf("%.3f", or_pa)`^10^ = **`r sprintf("%.2f", or_pa^10)`** — the odds
over half as big again.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
**And note Progress 8 has changed.** On its own it was
`r sprintf("%.3f", exp(g1))`; here it is `r sprintf("%.3f", or_p8)`. Same
arithmetic, **different claim** — this one holds absence, disadvantage, size
and school type constant. Always say which one you mean.
:::

## Reading odds ratios {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: 92%

or_tbl <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(logit_below)),
  est  = coef(logit_below),
  se   = summary(logit_below)$coefficients[, 2]
) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(or = exp(est), lo = exp(est - 1.96 * se), hi = exp(est + 1.96 * se),
         term = recode(term,
           "P8MEA" = "Progress 8",
           "PTFSM6CLA1A" = "% disadvantaged",
           "PERCTOT" = "% overall absence",
           "PPERSABS10" = "% persistently absent",
           "log(TPUP)" = "log(cohort size)",
           "PTPRIORHI" = "% high prior attainers",
           "MINORGROUPMaintained school" = "Maintained (vs academy)"))

ggplot(or_tbl, aes(x = or, y = fct_reorder(term, or))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = casa_red, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.25, colour = casa_purple) +
  geom_point(size = 3.4, colour = casa_teal) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio (log scale)", y = NULL,
       title = "Odds of being rated below Good",
       subtitle = "Left of the dashed line = protective; right = raises the odds")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
Anything whose interval crosses **1** is doing nothing detectable. Note
how much work Progress 8 is doing compared with everything else.
:::

## How do you score a model like this? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

For three weeks we judged models with **R²** — the share of the variation in
the outcome the model managed to explain.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
That worked because the outcome was a *number*, with variation in it to
explain. Ours is a **yes or no**. There is no spread to account for, and R²
as you know it simply does not exist here.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
So we ask **two** questions instead, and they are genuinely different:

1.  **Does the model fit the data?** — likelihood, deviance, AIC, the
    pseudo-R²s, Hosmer–Lemeshow
2.  **Does it make good decisions?** — accuracy, the confusion matrix, ROC
    and AUC

A model can do respectably on one and badly on the other. We take them in
turn.
:::

# 1. Does the model fit? {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Likelihood: the probability of what happened {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: fit-stats
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
n_tr   <- nrow(train)
ll     <- as.numeric(logLik(logit_below))
dev0   <- logit_below$null.deviance
dev1   <- logit_below$deviance
k      <- length(coef(logit_below))
cs     <- 1 - exp((dev1 - dev0) / n_tr)
cs_max <- 1 - exp(-dev0 / n_tr)
nk     <- cs / cs_max
```

Every school in the data **either was or was not** rated below Good — no
ambiguity. And the model gives every school a probability. So we can ask one
question of each school in turn:

> *What probability did the model put on the thing that actually happened?*

```{r}
#| label: likelihood-examples
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
p_tr <- fitted(logit_below)

# Three real training schools. Picked as the rows nearest a target
# probability rather than the extremes, because the extremes round to 0.00
# and 1.00 and look invented.
pick <- function(outcome, target) {
  idx <- which(train$below_good == outcome)
  idx[which.min(abs(p_tr[idx] - target))]
}
i1 <- pick(1, 0.80)   # struggling school, called correctly
i2 <- pick(0, 0.05)   # healthy school, called correctly
i3 <- pick(1, 0.03)   # struggling school the model was confident about - wrongly

idx3 <- c(i1, i2, i3)
truth_p <- ifelse(train$below_good[idx3] == 1, p_tr[idx3], 1 - p_tr[idx3])

ex <- tibble(
  School = c("A", "B", "C"),
  `What actually happened` = ifelse(train$below_good[idx3] == 1,
                                    "Below Good", "Good or better"),
  `Model's P(below Good)` = sprintf("%.2f", p_tr[idx3]),
  `Probability it put on what happened` = sprintf("**%.2f**", truth_p)
)
kable(ex, align = "cllr")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.86em"}
**The last column is the whole idea.** For **A** and **B** the model was
confident and right, so it put a high probability on the truth. For **C** it
was confident and *wrong* — it gave that school
only `r sprintf("%.2f", p_tr[i3])` of being below Good, and below Good is exactly
what it was.
:::

## From three schools to one number {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Do that for **every** school, then **multiply the last column together**. That
product is the **likelihood** of the whole dataset.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
And now the definition of fitting falls out of it:

> **Fitting the model *is* choosing the coefficients that make that number as
> large as possible.**

That is all **maximum likelihood** means. There is no formula to solve as
there was in OLS — the computer searches until it cannot make the number any
bigger.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
We report its **log**, for a blunt practical reason: multiplying
`r comma(n_tr)` numbers that are all smaller than 1 gives a result far too
small for a computer to hold. Taking logs turns that product into a sum.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true
logLik(logit_below)
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.86em"}
**Always negative, and closer to zero is better.** You will also hear this
described as how *surprised* the model is: school **C** above was a nasty
surprise, and surprises are what drag the number down.
:::

## Deviance: distance from a perfect fit {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

A log-likelihood on its own is hard to read. **Deviance** rescales it into
something more like an error score — *how far this model sits from one that
predicted every school perfectly*.

$$\text{deviance} = -2 \times \text{log-likelihood}$$

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
| | | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **Null deviance** | `r sprintf("%.1f", dev0)` | with **no predictors at all** — just the overall rate |
| **Residual deviance** | `r sprintf("%.1f", dev1)` | with our seven predictors in |
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true
logit_below$null.deviance    # no predictors
logit_below$deviance         # our model
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Lower is better**, and the drop — `r sprintf("%.0f", dev0 - dev1)` — is what
the predictors bought us. This is the direct equivalent of the sum-of-squares
drop you used to read off an OLS table.
:::

::: {.notes}
Deviance is also the statistic behind the overdispersion check later in the
Poisson section: residual deviance divided by residual degrees of freedom.
Worth flagging forward so it is not a surprise there.
:::

## AIC: fit, minus a fine for complexity {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

There is a problem with judging a model on deviance alone: **adding any
predictor, however useless, will always lower it slightly.** Left to itself,
deviance always says "more variables".

. . .

So we charge for them:

$$\text{AIC} = \text{deviance} + 2k \quad\text{where } k = \text{number of coefficients}$$

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
For our model: `r sprintf("%.1f", dev1)` + 2 × `r k` =
**`r sprintf("%.1f", dev1 + 2*k)`**. A predictor only improves the AIC if it
reduces the deviance by more than the 2 points it costs.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true
AIC(logit_below)
```

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
**AIC has no meaning on its own.** `r sprintf("%.0f", AIC(logit_below))` is
neither good nor bad — it is only useful for **comparing models fitted to the
same data**. Lower wins. That is exactly how we used it earlier to choose
between a raw and a logged predictor.
:::

## The pseudo-R²s {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

People badly want an R², so several substitutes exist. The two you will meet
in software output:

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Cox & Snell** — built from the likelihood ratio between your model and the
null model. For us: **`r sprintf("%.3f", cs)`**.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
That looks dismal — until you learn its catch. **Cox & Snell cannot reach 1.**
With a binary outcome its ceiling here is **`r sprintf("%.3f", cs_max)`**, so
`r sprintf("%.3f", cs)` is really `r sprintf("%.3f", cs)` out of a possible
`r sprintf("%.3f", cs_max)`.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Nagelkerke** fixes precisely that, by dividing by the ceiling:

$$R^2_{\text{Nagelkerke}} = \frac{`r sprintf("%.3f", cs)`}{`r sprintf("%.3f", cs_max)`} = \mathbf{`r sprintf("%.3f", nk)`}$$

Now it can reach 1, and it reads much more like the R² you are used to.
:::

## Getting them in R {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Unlike `logLik()`, `AIC()` and the deviances, the pseudo-R²s are **not in base
R** — `summary()` will not give you one. The `performance` package will:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
performance::r2_coxsnell(logit_below)
performance::r2_nagelkerke(logit_below)
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
So the whole fit toolkit is four lines:

| What | How |
|---|---|
| Log-likelihood | `logLik(model)` |
| Deviances | `model$null.deviance`, `model$deviance` |
| AIC | `AIC(model)` |
| Pseudo-R² | `performance::r2_nagelkerke(model)` |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
`summary(model)` prints the deviances and the AIC for you at the bottom of its
output — you have been looking at them all along without knowing what they
were.
:::

## ...and the same four in Python {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

In `statsmodels` the first three are **attributes** of the fitted model rather
than functions — no brackets:

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
| What | R | Python (`statsmodels`) |
|---|---|---|
| Log-likelihood | `logLik(model)` | `model.llf` |
| Deviances | `model$null.deviance` / `model$deviance` | `model.null_deviance` / `model.deviance` |
| AIC | `AIC(model)` | `model.aic` |
| Pseudo-R² | `performance::r2_nagelkerke(model)` | **nothing built in** |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
For the pseudo-R²s you write them out. Two lines, and they agree with
`performance` to six decimal places:

```python
n   = model.nobs
cs  = 1 - np.exp((model.llnull - model.llf) * 2 / n)   # Cox & Snell
nag = cs / (1 - np.exp(2 * model.llnull / n))          # Nagelkerke
```
:::

## One trap worth knowing about {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Fit with `smf.logit()` instead of `smf.glm()` and Python *does* hand you a
`.prsquared`. It is tempting. **Do not assume it is the one we just
calculated.**
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
`.prsquared` is **McFadden's** pseudo-R² — a different measure, built a
different way. On our model:

| | |
|---|---|
| Nagelkerke | **`r sprintf("%.3f", nk)`** |
| McFadden (`.prsquared`) | **`r sprintf("%.3f", 1 - ll / (-dev0 / 2))`** |
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:10px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.92em;"}
Same data, same model, same fit — **different number**, because they are
different quantities with the same nickname.

Whichever you report, **name it**. "Pseudo-R² = 0.3" tells your reader almost
nothing on its own.
:::

## ...and how much to trust them {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Report them if the journal or the marker expects them — but know what you are
saying.

::: incremental
-   **They are not "variance explained".** Nothing here is variance. The name
    is borrowed, and the interpretation does not come with it
-   **They are not comparable across datasets**, and barely across models. A
    Nagelkerke of 0.32 is not "half as good" as one of 0.64
-   **There is no accepted threshold** for a good one. Values that would be
    embarrassing in OLS are routine here
:::
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
Treat a pseudo-R² as a **rough indication that the predictors are doing
something**, and nothing more. If you want to know whether the model is
actually any use, ask the second question — the one we come to next.
:::

# 2. Does it make good decisions? {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Pause — this part is not just for logistic regression {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Everything in this section applies to **any model you will ever fit** — the OLS
models from Vol 1 and 2, the mixed effects models from Vol 3, and every machine
learning method you go on to meet.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**What transfers, unchanged:**

- **Hold data back.** Fit on some, judge on the rest. A model marked on its own
  training data flatters itself, whatever kind of model it is
- **Compare against a baseline.** Never ask *"is this good?"* — ask *"is this
  better than the dumbest thing I could have done?"*
- **Fit and prediction are different questions.** A model can describe this
  data well and still be useless on the next school
:::

## ...but the scoreboard changes {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

**What does *not* transfer is how you keep score.** Accuracy, the confusion
matrix and AUC all need a **categorical** outcome — none of them means
anything if you are predicting a number.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Swap the outcome type and you swap the metric:

| If the outcome is… | Baseline to beat | Typical metrics |
|---|---|---|
| A **category** | always predict the commonest class | accuracy, AUC, precision/recall |
| A **number** | always predict the mean | RMSE, MAE, R² **on held-out data** |
| A **count** | always predict the mean count | RMSE, or deviance on held-out data |
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.88em;"}
So learn the **shape** of what follows, not just the logistic version of it.
We come back to what this means for the earlier lectures at the end.
:::

## A recipe for judging the decisions {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Same shape as the fit recipe. **Six steps, and the order matters:**

::: {.incremental}
1.  **Hold data back** — fit on some schools, judge on the rest
2.  **Predict** on the ones it never saw
3.  **Compare against a baseline** — never quote accuracy on its own
4.  **Read the confusion matrix** — *which kind* of mistake is it making?
5.  **Check the ranking with AUC** — this needs no cut-off at all
6.  **Only then pick a cut-off** — and that is a policy decision, not a
    statistical one
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
Steps 5 and 6 are the ones people skip, and they are where the interesting
part lives.
:::

## First, the thing we are guarding against {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Here are fifteen points, and two models fitted to them. The **red** one is
better at its job — it passes through every single point and makes **no error
at all**.

```{r}
#| label: overfitting-figure
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 4.1
#| out-width: 95%

set.seed(11)
truth_fn <- function(x) 20 + 6 * x - 0.45 * x^2
n_of  <- 15
x_fit  <- sort(runif(n_of, 0.3, 9.7))
d_fit  <- tibble(x = x_fit, y = truth_fn(x_fit) + rnorm(n_of, 0, 3.2))
x_new  <- sort(runif(n_of, 0.3, 9.7))
d_new  <- tibble(x = x_new, y = truth_fn(x_new) + rnorm(n_of, 0, 3.2))

simple_fit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 2), data = d_fit)
# An interpolating spline: it is *forced* through every training point, which
# is precisely the behaviour we want to put on screen.
wiggly_fit <- splinefun(d_fit$x, d_fit$y, method = "fmm")

# Bounded by the training points: past the last knot the spline extrapolates
# cubically and dives off the bottom of the panel, which looks like a fault.
gx <- seq(min(d_fit$x), max(d_fit$x), length.out = 500)
curves <- bind_rows(
  tibble(x = gx, y = predict(simple_fit, newdata = tibble(x = gx)),
         Model = "Simple model"),
  tibble(x = gx, y = wiggly_fit(gx), Model = "Wiggly model"))

rmse_of <- function(a, b) sqrt(mean((a - b)^2))
of_panel <- function(d, title, e_simple, e_wiggly) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_line(data = curves, aes(x, y, colour = Model), linewidth = 1.15) +
    geom_point(data = d, aes(x, y), size = 2.9, colour = "grey15") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("Simple model" = casa_teal,
                                   "Wiggly model" = casa_red)) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(15, 50)) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL,
         subtitle = sprintf("average error —  simple: %.2f      wiggly: %.2f",
                            e_simple, e_wiggly)) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11))
}

e1s <- rmse_of(d_fit$y, predict(simple_fit, d_fit))
e1w <- rmse_of(d_fit$y, wiggly_fit(d_fit$x))
e2s <- rmse_of(d_new$y, predict(simple_fit, d_new))
e2w <- rmse_of(d_new$y, wiggly_fit(d_new$x))

(of_panel(d_fit, "Fitted on these 15 points", e1s, e1w) |
 of_panel(d_new, "Then shown 15 it had never seen", e2s, e2w)) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.86em"}
On the **left** the red model is flawless and the teal one is not. On the
**right** — the same two models, fifteen points neither has seen — the red one
is now **the worse of the two**, by a distance.
:::

## Overfitting {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
The red model did not learn the **pattern**. It learned the **noise** — the
particular wobbles of the particular fifteen points it was handed, which the
next fifteen do not share.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
And here is the uncomfortable part. **You can always make the fit better.**
Add a predictor, add an interaction, add a squared term — the fit to the data
in front of you never gets worse. Push it far enough and you reach error
`r sprintf("%.2f", e1w)`, like the red line.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:10px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.95em;"}
So **"it fits well" is not evidence of very much on its own** — and a *perfect*
fit is not a triumph, it is a warning sign.

The only honest test is data the model has **never seen**. Which is exactly
what we do next.
:::

## Steps 1 and 2: don't mark your own homework {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

So we split the schools **before** fitting anything: learn from one part,
judge on the other.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- sample(nrow(model_data), floor(0.7 * nrow(model_data)))
train <- model_data[train_idx, ]   # fit the model on these
test  <- model_data[-train_idx, ]  # judge it on these
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
`r comma(nrow(train))` schools to **learn** from. `r comma(nrow(test))` kept
back to **test** on.

**Test-set accuracy** is then one question: of the `r comma(nrow(test))`
schools the model never met, what share did it get right?
:::

## Step 3: so how good is it? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The model gives every school a **probability**. To count how often it is
*right*, we need a **cut-off** to turn those into yes/no answers.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
# p_below is introduced to students in the echoed chunk below, but the note
# above it needs the counts first, so they are worked out quietly here.
n_flag_half <- sum(predict(logit_below, newdata = test, type = "response") > 0.5)
n_test      <- nrow(test)
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
We will use **0.5** — *50% of the time*. We could choose any threshold - 10%, 90% etc. we will come back to this at step 6.

It is applied **school by school**, so it does not flag half the schools: at
0.5 it flags `r n_flag_half` of `r comma(n_test)`.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
p_below  <- predict(logit_below, newdata = test, type = "response")
accuracy <- mean((p_below > 0.5) == test$below_good)
baseline <- max(mean(test$below_good), 1 - mean(test$below_good))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
auc_below <- auc_of(p_below, test$below_good)
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em"}
**Test-set accuracy: `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * accuracy)`** — nearly nine
schools in ten.
:::

. . .

::: {.fragment style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #C94C4C"}
**Now watch.**
:::

## The single most important slide today {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| out-width: 88%

tibble(
  model = c("Our logistic model", "A model that always\nsays 'not below Good'"),
  acc   = c(accuracy, baseline)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_rev(model), y = 100 * acc, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * acc)), hjust = -0.15, size = 6) +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Our logistic model" = casa_teal,
                               "A model that always\nsays 'not below Good'" = casa_red)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Test-set accuracy (%)",
       title = "Our model versus a model that does nothing at all") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
A model that makes **the same prediction every single time** scores
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * baseline)`. Ours beats it by
**`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (accuracy - baseline))` percentage points**.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
**And that red bar is a model you have already met.** `glm(below_good ~ 1)`
fits an intercept and nothing else, so it predicts the base rate —
`r sprintf("%.3f", mean(train$below_good))` — for every school. Under 0.5, so
it answers "not below Good" to all of them. Its deviance is the **null
deviance** (`r sprintf("%.0f", dev0)`) from the fit section: R has been
fitting this model for you every time you call `glm()`.
:::

## Step 4: why accuracy lied to us {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: confusion-pair
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: 94%

actual_lab <- ifelse(test$below_good == 1, "Below Good", "Good or better")
pred_ours  <- ifelse(p_below > 0.5, "Below Good", "Good or better")
pred_base  <- rep("Good or better", nrow(test))   # the do-nothing model

cm <- table(Actual = actual_lab, Predicted = pred_ours)

cm_tbl <- function(pred, label) {
  tibble(Actual = actual_lab, Predicted = pred) |>
    count(Actual, Predicted) |>
    # a cell with no schools in it still has to be drawn, and for the
    # baseline that is half the grid
    complete(Actual    = c("Below Good", "Good or better"),
             Predicted = c("Below Good", "Good or better"),
             fill = list(n = 0)) |>
    mutate(correct = Actual == Predicted, Model = label)
}

n_base <- sum(pred_base == actual_lab)
n_ours <- sum(pred_ours == actual_lab)
lab_b  <- sprintf("Baseline: always says \"Good or better\"\n%s of %s right  —  %.1f%%",
                  comma(n_base), comma(nrow(test)), 100 * n_base / nrow(test))
lab_o  <- sprintf("Our logistic model\n%s of %s right  —  %.1f%%",
                  comma(n_ours), comma(nrow(test)), 100 * n_ours / nrow(test))

bind_rows(cm_tbl(pred_base, lab_b), cm_tbl(pred_ours, lab_o)) |>
  mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = c(lab_b, lab_o))) |>
  ggplot(aes(Predicted, fct_rev(Actual), fill = correct)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 2.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(n)), size = 7, colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  facet_wrap(~ Model) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = casa_teal, `FALSE` = casa_red)) +
  labs(x = "Model predicted...", y = "Actually was...") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11.5, lineheight = 1.2))
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.78em"}
**Teal = right, red = wrong.** Both models are judged on the same
`r comma(nrow(test))` test schools.
:::

::: incremental
- The baseline **never flags a single school** — its entire left-hand column
  is zero — and still scores **`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * baseline)`**
- Ours flags `r cm["Below Good","Below Good"] + cm["Good or better","Below Good"]`
  schools and gets `r cm["Below Good","Below Good"]` of them right. **That is
  the whole of the `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (accuracy - baseline))`-point gain**
- It still misses `r cm["Below Good","Good or better"]` of the
  `r comma(sum(test$below_good))` really below Good — close to useless for
  deciding where to send inspectors *at this threshold*
:::

## Step 5: judge the ranking, not the labels {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Everything so far hung on **0.5** — and nothing made 0.5 the right cut-off.
Move it and the accuracy, the catches and the false alarms all move with it.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
So ask a question that **does not depend on the cut-off at all**:

> *Does the model put schools in the right **order**? Are the struggling ones
> nearer the top of the list than the healthy ones?*

A model that ranks well is useful whatever cut-off you eventually pick. That
is what **ROC** and **AUC** measure.
:::

## What a ROC curve actually is {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

**ROC** stands for **Receiver Operating Characteristic** — a name that makes
no sense until you know where it came from.

::: {style="font-size: 0.86em"}
It was invented by radar engineers during the Second World War. The *receiver*
was the radar set, and the problem was exactly ours: an operator watching a
screen has to decide what is a real aircraft and what is noise. Catch more
aircraft and you also raise more false alarms. Where you set that dial is the
*operating characteristic*.
:::

. . .

Same idea here. Slide the cut-off from 1 all the way down to 0, and at
**every** setting write down two numbers:

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
- **How many struggling schools did we catch?** *(of those that really are
  below Good — we want this high)*
- **How many healthy schools did we wrongly flag?** *(of those that are fine —
  we want this low)*
:::

```{r}
#| label: roc-explained
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-align: center
thr_all <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 400)
roc_df <- map_dfr(thr_all, function(t) {
  tibble(tpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 1] > t),
         fpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 0] > t))
})
marks <- map_dfr(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.1), function(t) {
  tibble(t = t,
         tpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 1] > t),
         fpr = mean(p_below[test$below_good == 0] > t))
})

ggplot(roc_df, aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = casa_teal, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = marks, colour = casa_red, size = 2.6) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(label = sprintf("cut-off %.1f", t)),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3, colour = casa_red) +
  labs(x = "Healthy schools wrongly flagged", y = "Struggling schools caught") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
Plot one against the other and you get the curve. **Each red dot is one
cut-off.** The dashed diagonal is what pure guessing would give you — the
further above it the curve sits, the more the model knows.
:::

## AUC — one number for the whole curve {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

A curve is awkward to quote in a sentence, so we summarise it by the **area
underneath it** — which is all **AUC** stands for: **Area Under the Curve**.
You will also see it written **AUROC**, *area under the ROC curve*; same thing.

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
| AUC | What it means |
|---|---|
| **0.5** | the diagonal — no better than tossing a coin |
| **0.7–0.8** | useful |
| **0.9+** | very strong |
| **1.0** | perfect — every struggling school ranked above every healthy one |
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
roc <- performance::performance_roc(logit_below, new_data = test)
bayestestR::area_under_curve(roc$Specificity, roc$Sensitivity)
```

## What our AUC says {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:11px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.9em;"}
**Ours is `r sprintf("%.3f", auc_below)`**, which reads as:

> *Pick one school that really is below Good and one that really is not. The
> model gives the struggling one the **higher predicted probability of being
> below Good** `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * auc_below)` of the time.*
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
**"Predicted probability" means the model's own output** — the 0-to-1 number
from `predict(..., type = "response")` that we have been cutting at 0.5. Not
Progress 8, and not any of the predictors: a *higher* number means *more
likely to be below Good*.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Remember accuracy said this model was barely better than useless. **It ranks
well; we were just reading it at the wrong cut-off.**
:::

## Step 6: now choose your cut-off {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The ROC curve showed you **every** cut-off at once. Choosing one just means
deciding **which point on that curve you want to sit at.**

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
Here are the three red dots from that curve, written out as counts:
:::

```{r}
#| label: threshold-table
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
map_dfr(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.1), function(t) {
  flag <- p_below > t
  tibble(`Flag if probability above` = sprintf("%.2f", t),
         `Struggling schools caught`  = sum(flag & test$below_good == 1),
         `...and missed`              = sum(!flag & test$below_good == 1),
         `False alarms`               = sum(flag & test$below_good == 0))
}) |> kable(align = "crrr")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
Lower the cut-off and you move **up and to the right** along the curve: more
struggling schools caught, more healthy ones wrongly flagged. **There is no
point on the curve that is simply best.**
:::

## The bit AUC cannot do for you {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**AUC told you the curve was worth picking from.** A model with an AUC of 0.5
has nothing to offer at *any* cut-off. Ours ranks well, so some point on it is
worth using.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**But AUC cannot tell you where to sit on it**, because that is not a
statistical question:

- If a missed school means children let down — **catch more**, and accept the
  false alarms.
- If a false alarm means a wasted inspection — **flag fewer**, and accept the
  misses.
:::

. . .

::: {.fragment style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #C94C4C"}
**The model cannot tell you which of those matters more. You have to.**
:::

# Wrapping up {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## The three you did not get today {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Everything we have done generalises, and **the hard part is behind you**. Each
of these is the same machinery with a different family:

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
| If your outcome is... | Use | And the coefficients are |
|---|---|---|
| An **ordered** category — Ofsted's four grades, a Likert scale | `MASS::polr()` | odds of landing in a *higher* category |
| An **unordered** category — which region, which destination | `nnet::multinom()` | odds against a reference category |
| A **count** — pupils excluded, schools below Good in an LA | `glm(family = poisson)` | **rate ratios**, read just like odds ratios |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
Two things to know if you reach for the count model:

-   An **offset** — `offset(log(pupils))` — turns a model of counts into a
    model of *rates*, which is almost always what you want
-   Check for **overdispersion** (residual deviance ÷ residual df). Much above
    1 and you want `quasipoisson` or `MASS::glm.nb()`
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.85em;"}
**The practical covers these**, and the reading goes further. You already have
the two ideas that make them work: a **link function**, and coefficients you
have to **exponentiate** before they mean anything.
:::

## The family, in one slide {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

| Outcome | `family =` | Link | Interpret coefficients as |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Continuous | `gaussian` | identity | Units of y per unit of x |
| Yes / no | `binomial` | logit | Odds ratios |
| x out of n | `binomial` | logit | Odds ratios |
| Ordered categories | `MASS::polr()` | logit | Odds of being in a higher category |
| Unordered categories | `nnet::multinom()` | logit | Odds vs a reference category |
| Count | `poisson` | log | Rate ratios |
| Overdispersed count | `MASS::glm.nb()` | log | Rate ratios |

. . .

**One framework.** Change the family, change the link, and everything
you learned about building and interpreting a linear model still
applies.

## What carried over, and what didn't {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Still true**

- The recipe: start simple, add complexity that earns its place
- Confounding, mediation, interactions
- Multicollinearity and VIF
- Thinking hard about what belongs in the model
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Different now**

- No R² - use AIC, deviance, or predictive performance
- Coefficients need exponentiating before they mean anything
- Residual plots look strange and need different diagnostics
- Accuracy is a trap on imbalanced outcomes
:::
:::::

## Where you can go next {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- **Generalised additive models (GAMs)** - when the relationship is
  smooth but not a straight line
- **`glmer()`** - the intersection of this week and last week: a GLM
  with random effects, for grouped non-normal data
- **Spatial and geographically weighted regression** - when the
  relationship itself varies over space
- **Ridge and lasso** - when you have too many predictors and need the
  model to choose

. . .

You now have the two big extensions to OLS: last week we relaxed
**independence**, this week we relaxed **normality**. Almost everything
else is a combination of the two.

## Explaining, or predicting? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Worth noticing what changed across these four sessions — because it was not
just the model.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Vols 1–3: explaining**

R², residual plots, VIF, AIC, significance.

Every one of those is computed on **the data you fitted to**. The question is
*does this model describe the process I am looking at?*
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Today: predicting**

Train/test split, accuracy against a baseline, AUC.

All computed on data the model **has never seen**. The question is *will this
work on the next school?*
:::
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"}
**Both are legitimate. They are not the same job**, and they can disagree — a
model packed with significant coefficients can predict badly, and a model that
predicts well can be uninterpretable.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
**Decide which one you are doing before you start**, because it changes what
counts as a good model. For the assessment, say which — *"I am explaining why
schools differ"* and *"I am predicting which schools will struggle"* are
different claims and need different evidence.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.52em; color:#666; margin-top:0.4em;"}
Shmueli, G. (2010) To Explain or to Predict? *Statistical Science*, **25**(3),
289–310.
[doi:10.1214/10-STS330](https://doi.org/10.1214/10-STS330)
:::

## So — can we predict School Ofsted ratings? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

We asked that on slide one. The honest answer is **partly**, and the model is
specific about which part.

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
| | Our model | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Ranking** — AUC | `r sprintf("%.3f", auc_below)` | Good. It puts a struggling school above a healthy one `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * auc_below)` of the time |
| **Labelling** — accuracy at 0.5 | `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * accuracy)` vs a do-nothing baseline of `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * baseline)` | Almost worthless |
| **Fit** — Nagelkerke R² | `r sprintf("%.3f", nk)` (Cox & Snell `r sprintf("%.3f", cs)`) | Respectable for cross-sectional social data |
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
And on the **variables**: Progress 8 dominates everything else
(OR `r sprintf("%.3f", or_p8)`), persistent absence adds a little per
percentage point (OR `r sprintf("%.3f", or_pa)`), and most of the rest have
intervals crossing 1 — *doing nothing detectable*.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.9em;"}
**In one line: a decent ranking device, and a poor labelling device.** Those
are different claims, and the deck spent an hour on why.
:::

## ...and here is what it cannot tell you {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.88em"}
::: incremental
-   **Circularity.** Inspectors read Progress 8 *before* they visit. We are
    not independently predicting a judgement — we are partly recovering one
    of its own inputs. Our strongest coefficient is the one we should trust
    least.
-   **Timing.** Ratings here span
    **`r min(model_data$insp_year, na.rm = TRUE)`–`r max(model_data$insp_year, na.rm = TRUE)`**;
    the results are 2022-23. Some ratings were handed out a decade *before*
    the data we are "predicting" them with.
-   **Causation.** Nothing here says that raising a school's Progress 8 would
    change its rating. We have an association, measured on log-odds.
-   **Rarity.** Only `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(model_data$below_good))`
    of schools are below Good. The model inherits that, and so does every
    accuracy figure you quote from it.
:::
:::

## The bit the software will never do for you {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
Every number on the last two slides is **correct**. The code ran, the maths
is right, the AUC is genuinely 0.82.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**None of it tells you whether the model is any use.** That verdict came from
knowing something R does not: *how an Ofsted inspection actually works*.
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#4e3c56; color:white; padding:11px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.95em;"}
These methods will carry you a long way, and they will show you things you
could not have seen by eye. But they measure **associations in the data you
happened to collect** — they cannot tell you where that data came from, who
made it, or what it would mean to act on it.

**That part is yours.** It always was.
:::

## Conclusions {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- **Look at your outcome variable before you choose a model.** Week 1's
  data types were not an academic exercise - they determine what you are
  allowed to do
- A GLM is not a new method, it is the same linear predictor with a
  different distribution and a link function bolted on
- **Always compare against a baseline.** A model that beats "predict the
  majority every time" by half a percentage point has not learned much
- Check your assumptions, and remember the threshold is a choice you
  make rather than one the model makes for you
- And ask where your predictors came from. Our best one turned out to be
  something Ofsted had already read

## Today's Practical {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

- Building and interpreting your own logistic and Poisson models on the
  schools data
- Practice at the bit that matters most: **interpreting odds ratios and
  rate ratios** in plain English
- And deciding, for an outcome of your own choosing, which member of the
  family you actually need
